name: Tristan da Cunha

pin.note: Approximate centre of the main island of Tristan da Cunha (NASA JPL gives about 37.1 S, 12.3 W)

territory: British Overseas Territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha

creatures.iucn_status: Critically Endangered (uplisted 2008; later assessment year not verified)
creatures.status_note: Breeds almost entirely on Gough Island; threatened by house mouse predation of chicks and longline bycatch; breeding success improved after the 2021 mouse eradication attempt but mice persist at low numbers.

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha's main settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, sits at about 37 degrees 4 minutes S, 12 degrees 18 minutes W in the South Atlantic.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha lies roughly 2,800 km from the southern tip of Africa and over 3,000 km from South America's east coast, with St Helena (about 2,173 km to the northeast) the nearest neighbour.
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Location paragraph of the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2012 UK Ministry of Defence article called Tristan da Cunha the most remote inhabited archipelago in the world, about 2,816 km from South Africa and 3,360 km from South America.
facts.source_title: Royal Navy surveys remote volcanic archipelago
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The territory has a total land area of about 207 km2, of which the main island accounts for about 98 km2.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha has a cool oceanic climate with mild temperatures and persistent westerly winds.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The annual mean daily maximum temperature is about 17.3 C and the mean daily minimum about 12.4 C.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Summer temperatures on Tristan do not reach 25 C, and frost does not occur below about 500 m elevation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha receives about 1,681 mm of rain a year spread over roughly 252 rainy days.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island gets about 1,498 hours of sunshine a year, around 34 percent of the possible total.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The main island is roughly 13 km wide and mostly ringed by steep cliffs, with lower beaches on its southern and north-northwestern sides.
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Size and shape description in the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Queen Mary's Peak, the summit of the island's volcano, rises to about 2,060 m (6,760 ft).
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Volcano description in the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island is a shield volcano built from silica-poor lava such as basalt, with eruptions from the summit crater, flank vents and small cinder cones.
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Volcano paragraph of the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Tristan group was built by a hotspot lying about 400 km east of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the main island's flanks carry more than 30 cinder cones.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Earth tremors from August 1961 preceded a lava dome that formed on 10 October 1961 a few hundred feet east of the village; a 1962 Royal Society team found lava had flowed north and east into the sea.
facts.evidence_note: Account of eruption and expedition findings.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Portuguese explorer Tristao da Cunha first recorded sighting the islands in 1506, and the main island carries his name.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The first undisputed landing was in 1643 by a Dutch East India Company crew, and the first permanent settler, Jonathan Lambert, arrived in December 1810.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Britain annexed the islands on 14 August 1816 as a dependency of the Cape Colony.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The settlement was founded in 1816 by Sergeant William Glass and renamed Edinburgh of the Seven Seas to honour Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, who visited in 1867.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: When the volcano threatened in October 1961, all 264 islanders left, spent a night on Nightingale Island, and were carried by the Dutch liner Tjisadane to Cape Town, then on to England.
facts.source_title: The Evacuation of Tristan da Cunha
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 1961 evacuees were taken to England; after the 1962 Royal Society expedition judged the settlement largely intact, most islanders returned in 1963, the first group in April and the rest in November.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha is part of the British Overseas Territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha under a constitution in force since 1 September 2009.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Local government is led by an appointed administrator advised by an Island Council of eight elected and three appointed members; Ian Lavarello became Chief Islander in March 2025.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2021 census counted 243 residents; the article gives 221-222 for 2026, about 1.3 people per km2.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Gough and Inaccessible Islands, part of Tristan da Cunha, were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1995 (extended in 2004) under criteria vii and x, covering 397,900 ha including marine areas.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cliffs on these islands host about 22 seabird species, including albatrosses, petrels and penguins.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Gough Island has two endemic land birds, the Gough moorhen and Gough bunting, plus 12 endemic plant species; Inaccessible Island holds the Inaccessible Rail, the world's smallest flightless bird.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha has important breeding grounds for petrels, albatrosses, penguins and shearwaters.
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife sentence in the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Tristan Marine Protection Zone, designated in November 2020, covers 687,247 km2 and is described as the largest no-take zone in the Atlantic.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: House mice, probably brought by 19th-century sailors, now eat seabird chicks on Gough Island and have begun attacking adult birds.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Besides mice on Gough, invasive plants such as Sagina procumbens and New Zealand flax threaten the sites, while Inaccessible Island has no introduced mammals.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In austral summer 2021 helicopters spread rodenticide bait across Gough Island in an RSPB-led programme with the Tristan government and community.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Gough and Inaccessible are a Nature Reserve under a 2006 ordinance and Ramsar sites, managed so that only research and weather monitoring are allowed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Tristan albatross (Diomedea dabbenena) is listed as Critically Endangered, a status reached in 2008 after earlier being Endangered.
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: In May 2008 the Tristan albatross was recategorised Critically Endangered by BirdLife International on behalf of IUCN because of mouse predation of chicks on Gough Island and longline fishing mortality.
facts.source_title: Tristan Albatross now Critically Endangered - but help on the horizon?
facts.publisher: Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP)
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: The Tristan albatross breeds almost entirely on Gough Island, part of the Tristan da Cunha group.
facts.evidence_note: Tristan albatross entry in the description.
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: Gough holds about 1,500 breeding pairs of Tristan albatross, with a pair breeding on Inaccessible Island in some years.
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: The Tristan albatross breeds every second year, is monogamous, typically starts breeding around age 10, and has a wingspan up to about 3.05 m.
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: After the 2021 mouse operation, Tristan albatross breeding success on Gough reached 76 percent in 2022, up from a mouse-affected average of 32 percent, with over 1,000 chicks fledged.
facts.source_title: Gough Island's seabirds bounce back after rodent eradication
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: A survey reported in October 2021 gave island-wide Tristan albatross chick survival of 39.7 percent versus 37.2 percent the year before, with the RSPB noting mice still caused heavy losses.
facts.source_title: Annual Tristan albatross survey reveals mixed results
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: GBIF accepts Diomedea dabbenena Mathews, 1929 as a species, with taxon key 5722866.
facts.subject: tristan-albatross

facts.statement: MacGillivray's prion (Pachyptila macgillivrayi) is described as globally Critically Endangered by the IUCN World Heritage Outlook; the vast majority of its world population breeds on Gough Island, where its numbers are reported as declining and the smaller prions as likely facing extinction.
facts.evidence_note: Threatened-species and values sections of the assessment; the page also names mouse predation plus long-line fishing as risks of extinction for this prion and the Tristan albatross.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The spectacled petrel (Procellaria conspicillata) nests only on the high western plateau of Inaccessible Island and is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia, with a population estimated at 31,000 to 45,000 birds after downlisting from critically endangered (2000) to vulnerable (2007).
facts.evidence_note: Infobox and 'Conservation' section. IUCN Outlook page separately says the Inaccessible population continues to increase.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The northern rockhopper penguin (Eudyptes moseleyi) is classified as Endangered (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia; more than 99 percent breed on Tristan da Cunha and Gough Island, and a 2009 study cited there found a 90 percent decline since the 1950s.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox, lead and 'Distribution and habitat'. Decline figure is the Wikipedia article's citation of a 2009 study.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Gough finch or Gough bunting (Rowettia goughensis) is described as Critically Endangered; its total population on Gough Island was estimated at 1,917 individuals in 2020 (95% CI 1,550-2,500), and its range may have shrunk by 50 percent.
facts.evidence_note: Population section on the Gough Finch. Elsewhere the same page calls the species Gough Bunting and says it recovered from a minor impact of the 2021 mouse operation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Gough moorhen (Gallinula comeri) became rare on Gough Island after the 2021 mouse eradication operation, with fewer than 20 birds in 2025 and only a single reproductive pair recorded until 2024; the IUCN Outlook says several thousand likely live on Tristan da Cunha, where it was introduced in the 1950s (another section estimates about 41,500 birds there).
facts.evidence_note: Mouse and invasive-species threat text. The same page elsewhere says the moorhen had 'bounced back' after 2021, so wording is internally inconsistent; the <20 figure is the specific 2025 count. Wikipedia lists the species as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1). Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Inaccessible Island rail (Laterallus rogersi) is endemic to Inaccessible Island, is the smallest living flightless bird at 13 to 15.5 cm long, and is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1); Wikipedia says its single small population would be threatened by the accidental introduction of mammalian predators such as rats or cats.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox, lead, 'Morphology' and conservation text. The IUCN Outlook page also labels it Vulnerable with a stable population. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The endemic Tristan thrush or starchy (Turdus eremita) is listed as Near Threatened (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia, with about 850 pairs on Inaccessible Island and roughly 6,000 birds for the whole group in the 1980s, and black rats on Tristan an ongoing threat.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox, 'Status and conservation' and 'Population' sections; the population is reported as stable. Figures are dated (1980s survey).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Phylica arborea is described by the IUCN World Heritage Outlook as globally Endangered and found on the Tristan da Cunha islands; on Inaccessible Island introduced scale insects have reduced Phylica fruit loads and killed trees.
facts.evidence_note: Flora section and Inaccessible Island invasive-species text. Wikipedia's Tristan page calls it native but not endemic to Tristan. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) pup production on Gough Island fell by 95 percent over 40 years according to a 2019 census cited by the IUCN Outlook, which says the population is verging on local extinction; the page gives roughly 50-100 seals there and states no Red List category for it.
facts.evidence_note: Marine mammals section. Gough is described as the northernmost breeding site for the species.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Mean surface (3-10 m) water temperatures measured around the Tristan islands were 14.9 C at Gough, 17.9 C at Inaccessible and Nightingale, and 18.6 C at Tristan da Cunha, with Gough waters colder and less saline.
facts.source_title: First quantification of subtidal community structure at Tristan da Cunha Islands in the remote South Atlantic: from kelp forests to the deep sea
facts.publisher: PLOS ONE (Caselle et al. 2018; PDF copy hosted by UCSB)
facts.evidence_note: Results, 'Temperature, salinity and dissolved oxygen'. These are survey measurements from the research expedition, not long-term climatological means.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Tristan, Inaccessible and Nightingale islands lie north of the Subtropical Convergence, while Gough Island sits on or below that front depending on the season, so Gough's sea surface is on average 3-4 C colder and likely richer in nutrients.
facts.source_title: First quantification of subtidal community structure at Tristan da Cunha Islands in the remote South Atlantic: from kelp forests to the deep sea
facts.publisher: PLOS ONE (Caselle et al. 2018; PDF copy hosted by UCSB)
facts.evidence_note: Study-area description in the Introduction; the paper describes the islands as sitting at the confluence of two major ocean currents.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2017 survey cited by the IUCN Outlook found microplastics in 15 of 19 seawater samples from around the northern Tristan islands and Gough, averaging between 0 and 2.3 pieces per litre.
facts.evidence_note: Garbage and solid waste threat text, which attributes the survey to National Geographic and cites Caselle et al. 2018. Secondary report of the survey figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Plastic bottles washing ashore on Inaccessible Island have doubled in arrival rate since 2018 (Ryan et al. 2024, as cited), and on Nightingale Island over 90 percent of sampled great shearwater chicks carried life-threatening amounts of plastic.
facts.evidence_note: Plastic pollution text; the shearwater finding is attributed to an IUCN consultation (2025) and is only stated to be 'almost certainly' mirrored on Inaccessible.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Tristan da Cunha Marine Protection Ordinance 2021 designated the Tristan da Cunha Marine Protection Zone, while the Fisheries Limits Ordinance 1983 (as amended) controls commercial fishing in the exclusive economic zone out to 200 nautical miles.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The MS Oliva shipwreck at Nightingale Island in March 2011 caused significant damage to wildlife including oiling of northern rockhopper penguins, and in October 2020 the rock lobster vessel MV GeoSearcher sank off the north-west coast of Gough Island with consequences that could not be assessed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tristan da Cunha's weather records show a record high of 24.4 C (February and March) and a record low of 4.6 C (August), with mean daily maxima ranging from 21.2 C in February to 14.2 C in August.
facts.evidence_note: Climate data table. Record values are as printed in the Wikipedia table (period of record not given there).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On Tristan da Cunha the wettest month is August (about 175 mm over 26 rainy days) and the driest is January (about 93 mm over 18 rainy days), within an annual total of about 1,681 mm.
facts.evidence_note: Climate data table. Annual figure matches existing TDC-008.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: An extratropical cyclone struck the Tristan da Cunha islands on 21 May 2001 with winds up to 190 km/h, severely damaging several structures and killing numerous cattle, which prompted emergency British aid.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On the Tristan da Cunha-Gough Islands ecoregion, snow is rare at sea level but can fall on the peaks between May and January, and annual precipitation averages 1,676 mm on Tristan versus 3,397 mm on Gough.
facts.source_title: Tristan da Cunha-Gough Islands shrub and grasslands
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph. The Gough Island article gives a different figure (about 3,000 mm average rainfall and 12 C average temperature), so Gough rainfall sources disagree.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The IUCN Outlook says temperatures on Gough Island have risen since 1963 and that predictions for the South Atlantic are scant, with general warming, wetter winters, drier summers and increased storminess the likely outcomes.
facts.evidence_note: Climate change threat text and 'Potential threats' paragraph; the impact assessment is labelled Data Deficient.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sea conditions around Tristan da Cunha are described as notoriously rough, with storms, large waves and very high winds common enough that fishing is often limited to about 60 days per year.
facts.source_title: First quantification of subtidal community structure at Tristan da Cunha Islands in the remote South Atlantic: from kelp forests to the deep sea
facts.publisher: PLOS ONE (Caselle et al. 2018; PDF copy hosted by UCSB)
facts.evidence_note: Discussion of kelp growth form and wave exposure. Figure is stated as 'often limiting fishing opportunities to ~60 days per year'.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Gough Island has 26 flowering plant species (21 endemic to the Tristan group) and 27 fern species (15 endemic), while Inaccessible Island has 213 plant species, 10 found only there and 60 restricted to the archipelago.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: About 100 invertebrate species are recorded from Gough Island, 22 of them endemic to the island or the Tristan archipelago, and Inaccessible Island has at least 10 endemic invertebrates.
facts.evidence_note: Autochthonous terrestrial fauna section. The same page counts 130 moss species with 59 endemic in one study and 305 bryophytes with 86 endemic in another, so moss counts differ by study.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Nearshore reefs of the Tristan group are dominated by giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) forests reaching 30-40 m depth, with low biodiversity and a very simple food web, and the Tristan rock lobster (Jasus tristani) fishery provides about 80 percent of islanders' income.
facts.source_title: First quantification of subtidal community structure at Tristan da Cunha Islands in the remote South Atlantic: from kelp forests to the deep sea
facts.publisher: PLOS ONE (Caselle et al. 2018; PDF copy hosted by UCSB)
facts.evidence_note: Introduction and Discussion. The paper elsewhere says 80-90 percent of income; both ranges appear in the text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On Tristan da Cunha the endemic Tristan moorhen is extinct, eight Gough moorhens released at Sandy Point in 1956 colonised the island, and the South American silver porgy (Diplodus argenteus), thought to have sought refuge there after a 2006 oil-platform wreck, is suspected of consuming components of the kelp forest.
facts.evidence_note: 'Fauna' sections (Land and Marine). Silver porgy kelp impact is only 'suspected'; the IUCN Outlook page also reports porgy and variable blenny established on the northern islands and a reported klipfish decline. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On Inaccessible Island, the share of monitored Phylica trees infected with scale insects rose from 29 percent in 2011 to 85-100 percent in 2018, many of the largest trees died, and the large-billed Inaccessible Island finch (Nesospiza acunhae dunnei) fell by over 80 percent at its main monitoring site.
facts.evidence_note: Autochthonous fauna and invasive-species text. Another paragraph on the same page says the finch declined 50 percent in ten years, so the decline figure differs by section.
facts.subject: island
